passages.t: Seen from a window at dusk
passages.happening:
‘My son, keep my words and treasure my commandments within you’ (verse 1). ‘Keep my commandments and live; guard my teachings as the apple of your eye’ (verse 2). He should tell wisdom that she is his sister, ‘and call understanding your kinsman’ (verse 4), so that they keep him from the adulteress (verse 5).

Then the father tells a story. ‘For at the window of my house I looked through the lattice’ (verse 6). Among the simple he noticed ‘a young man lacking judgment’ (verse 7), ‘crossing the street near her corner, strolling down the road to her house’ (verse 8), ‘at twilight, as the day was fading into the dark of the night’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
This is the third and fullest warning about the forbidden woman in chapters 5 to 7. Chapter 5 told the cost and chapter 6 compared adultery to holding fire. Chapter 7 tells a single evening from start to finish, like a short play.

The apple of the eye is the pupil, ishon in Hebrew, the small, precious, carefully protected center of sight. The father's teaching is to be guarded that closely.

Calling wisdom ‘sister’ uses the language of family closeness, and in the Song of Songs sister is also a word for a bride. The father wants his son so close to wisdom that a stranger's advances find no room.

Houses in Israelite towns often had small windows with wooden lattices, which let in air and light and let those inside look out without being seen. The father is an unseen witness. And twilight was when the streets emptied, with no lamps to light them. A young man strolling near that corner at that hour was going where he had no business being. Nothing has happened yet. But he has already chosen the road.
passages.later: The psalmist prays in the same words: ‘Keep me as the apple of Your eye; hide me in the shadow of Your wings’ (Psalm 17:8). And Moses told Israel to keep God's words close in the same way: ‘tie them as reminders on your hands and bind them on your foreheads’ (Deuteronomy 11:18).
passages.asks: The young man's fall began with a walk he did not need to take. Ask where your own evenings tend to take you, and whether any of those roads lead toward a corner you know you should avoid. And ask what it would mean to treat wisdom as close family.

passages.t: Her offer, and the ox to the slaughter
passages.happening:
‘Then a woman came out to meet him, with the attire of a harlot and cunning of heart’ (verse 10). She is loud and defiant, and she lurks in the streets and squares (verses 11-12). She takes hold of him and kisses him, and brazenly makes her offer (verse 13).

“I have made my peace offerings; today I have paid my vows” (verse 14), she says. She came out looking for him. She has made her bed ready with ‘colored linen from Egypt’ (verse 16) and perfumed it with myrrh, aloes and cinnamon (verse 17). She invites him to spend the night with her. Her husband is away on business, she says, with a bag of money, and will not be home until the full moon (verses 19-20).

‘With her great persuasion she entices him; with her flattering lips she lures him’ (verse 21). ‘He follows her on impulse, like an ox going to the slaughter, like a deer bounding into a trap’ (verse 22), like a bird darting into a snare, not knowing it will cost him his life (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Every detail of her speech is chosen. Peace offerings were sacrifices in which part of the animal was burned on the altar, part given to the priest, and the rest eaten by the worshiper's household. The meat had to be eaten quickly (Leviticus 7:15-18). So when she says she has paid her vows, she means she has fresh meat at home and a feast ready, a rare luxury for most people.

Linen from Egypt, myrrh, aloes and cinnamon were costly goods brought in by trade from Egypt, Arabia and farther east. They signal wealth and a carefully prepared seduction. A husband away with a bag of money, not due back until the full moon, sounds like a merchant on a trading trip. No one will catch them.

The story slows down while she talks and then speeds up as he follows. Three pictures from the animal world end it: an ox, a deer, a bird. None of them knows what is coming. That is the young man's tragedy. He thinks he is choosing pleasure. He is walking into a trap.
passages.later: James describes the same evening in a sentence: ‘But each one is tempted when by his own evil desires he is lured away and enticed. Then after desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death’ (James 1:14-15). And Paul promises that no one is left without a way out: ‘But when you are tempted, He will also provide an escape, so that you can stand up under it’ (1 Corinthians 10:13).
passages.hard:
Why does the woman mention sacrifices and vows just before inviting the young man to her bed?

Her words in verse 14 are one of the chapter's most unsettling details. At the simplest level they explain the feast: peace offerings left the worshiper with meat that had to be eaten quickly, so she has a banquet ready.

But the mention also shows how easily religious practice can sit beside a plan to sin, and even dress it up. She has kept her vows at the sanctuary, and in the same breath she proposes adultery.

Readers explain it in different ways. Some scholars have suggested the scene reflects foreign cults in which sacred rites and sexual acts were linked. Some see the woman as a picture of idolatry itself, since the prophets often describe unfaithfulness to God as adultery. Others think the passage simply exposes religious hypocrisy of an ordinary kind. The text does not settle which. Its warning is clear on any reading: outward religious practice is no proof of a faithful heart.
passages.asks: The young man never saw the trap until it closed. Ask which pleasures in your life are dressed up to look harmless, or even religious. And ask God, who promises a way of escape, to show you where it is before the moment comes.

passages.t: Her house is the road to Sheol
passages.happening:
The father turns from the story to his sons. ‘Now, my sons, listen to me, and attend to the words of my mouth’ (verse 24). ‘Do not let your heart turn aside to her ways; do not stray into her paths’ (verse 25).

‘For she has brought many down to death; her slain are many in number’ (verse 26). ‘Her house is the road to Sheol, descending to the chambers of death’ (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is built around houses. It begins at the father's house, where he watches from the window. It follows the young man to the woman's house. And it ends by showing what her house really is: not a place of pleasure but a road down to the realm of the dead. Sheol is the Hebrew name for the grave, pictured as a place of the dead below the earth.

The warning starts with the heart, as chapter 4 said it must. The young man's feet went where his heart had already turned.

This scene prepares for chapters 8 and 9, where two women call out to the simple: Wisdom, whose house leads to life, and Folly, whose guests are in the depths of Sheol (9:18). The woman of chapter 7 is the living picture of what Folly will say.
passages.later: The Bible remembers that even Solomon, the wisest of kings, was led astray by the women he loved (1 Kings 11:1-4). Nehemiah later asks, ‘Did not King Solomon of Israel sin in matters like this?’ (Nehemiah 13:26).
passages.asks: The father says many strong people have been brought down this way. Ask whether you have been trusting your own strength to keep you safe. And if you have already walked this road, remember that the father's whole aim is to turn people back toward life, and ask whom you could speak to honestly about it.
